sections.content: The early 1970s marked a revolutionary period for music documentaries, with Gimme Shelter (1970) setting a new standard for capturing both the electricity and darkness of rock culture. D.A. Pennebaker's Don't Look Back (1967) had earlier established an influential cinéma vérité approach to filming musicians on tour, following Bob Dylan with unprecedented intimacy. These films moved beyond simple performance documentation to reveal complex personalities and cultural tensions.

sections.content: Martin Scorsese's The Last Waltz (1978) elevated the concert film genre through masterful cinematography and intimate backstage moments. The film demonstrated how thoughtful direction could transform live performance documentation into lasting cinematic art. This influenced later works like Jonathan Demme's Stop Making Sense (1984), which brought similar artistic ambition to filming Talking Heads. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Music Documentary Filmmaking

By the 1980s and 90s, music documentaries expanded beyond just concert footage. Madonna: Truth or Dare (1991) mixed performance with behind-the-scenes access, while Meeting People Is Easy (1998) captured Radiohead's growing disillusionment with fame. These films revealed how the genre could explore deeper themes about artistry, celebrity, and the toll of public life.
